column1: # Fair, original-words summaries of each approved tradition's view on a contested point.
# Written by Claude from the traditions' historic confessions and teachers; status 'draft' until Dave reviews them.
# Each tradition also contains a range of opinion; the summaries describe the main historic position.

column4: Baptists teach "believer's baptism": baptism is for those who have personally repented and put their faith in Christ, and it is done by immersing the whole body in water, picturing death, burial and resurrection with Christ. Baptism is an ordinance of obedience and a public confession of faith; it does not itself save or convey grace, but follows salvation. Because infants cannot yet believe, they are not baptized; many Baptist churches hold a service of dedication instead, and a person baptized as an infant is baptized as a believer.

Methodists and Wesleyans treat baptism as a sacrament: an outward sign of an inward grace and a means by which God works. It marks entry into the church and God's covenant, and it is given both to adults who come to faith and to the infants of Christian families. Pouring or sprinkling is usual, though immersion is also accepted. John Wesley linked baptism with the new birth, but taught that every baptized person must still personally turn to Christ and be born of the Spirit; baptized children are later confirmed in their own profession of faith.

Presbyterian and Reformed churches teach that baptism is a sacrament, a sign and seal of God's covenant of grace, which in the New Testament takes the place of circumcision. It is given to those who profess faith and also to the children of believing parents, because God's covenant promise is "unto you, and to your children" (Acts 2:39). Sprinkling or pouring is usual and immersion is valid. The grace signified is not tied to the moment of baptism and is received by faith; baptism does not automatically regenerate, and it is administered only once.

Lutherans teach that baptism is a means of grace: not simply water, but water joined to God's command and promise. Through it God gives forgiveness of sins, rescue from death and the devil, and eternal salvation to all who believe. Faith receives the gift, and God works faith even in infants through his Word, so children are baptized. The Augsburg Confession calls baptism necessary to salvation (while Lutherans do not teach that the unbaptized who believe are lost). Pouring is the usual mode. The baptized person returns daily to baptism by repentance and faith.

Most Pentecostal churches (for example the Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church) practise believer's baptism by immersion, much as Baptists do: an act of obedience and public testimony by those who have been born again, not a means of salvation. Infants are dedicated, not baptized. Pentecostals give special emphasis to a second, distinct "baptism in the Holy Spirit" (see the lesson on spiritual gifts). A minority ("Oneness" Pentecostals) baptize in the name of Jesus only; most Pentecostals use the threefold name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Many Baptists have historically held that the miraculous "sign" gifts (speaking in tongues, prophecy as new revelation, and gifts of healing and miracles) served to confirm the apostles' message and ceased once the New Testament was complete. God still heals and works in answer to prayer, and every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, with gifts for service such as teaching, giving and helping. Baptist views today vary widely: some churches are "continuationist" and open to all the gifts, as long as they are exercised in order and tested by Scripture.

Wesleyans emphasize the Spirit's work in making believers holy and filling them with love. John Wesley thought the extraordinary gifts had become rare in the church mainly because Christians had grown cold, not because God had withdrawn them, and he did not rule them out. The Holiness movement that grew out of Methodism taught a second work of grace, and Pentecostalism later grew from it. Methodists today hold a range of views; most stress the fruit of the Spirit over the extraordinary gifts, while a charismatic stream welcomes them.

The historic Reformed position is "cessationist": the revelatory and miraculous gifts (tongues, prophecy, miracles) belonged to the founding age of the apostles, confirming their message, and ceased when Scripture was complete; the Westminster Confession speaks of God's former ways of revealing his will as "now ceased." The Spirit continues to give gifts for teaching, serving and leading, and God still answers prayer for the sick in his providence. Some Reformed Christians today ("Reformed charismatics") hold that the gifts continue.

Lutherans teach that the Holy Spirit works through the means God has given, the Word and the Sacraments, to create and strengthen faith. Luther strongly opposed the "enthusiasts" who claimed the Spirit spoke to them directly apart from Scripture. The extraordinary gifts are not denied as possible, but they are not expected as normal, are not a sign of a higher Christian life, and must never be set beside or above the Word. Christians pray for healing and trust God's will; a charismatic movement has existed among some Lutherans since the 1960s.

Pentecostals teach that all the gifts of the Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy and healing, continue today. Classical Pentecostals (such as the Assemblies of God) teach a "baptism in the Holy Spirit" distinct from and usually after conversion, giving power for witness and service, with speaking in other tongues as its first outward sign. Divine healing is believed to be provided for in Christ's atoning work. The wider charismatic movement in many denominations welcomes the gifts but does not always teach tongues as the necessary sign of Spirit baptism.
